content: The provided text is a long list of references, primarily related to HIV/AIDS research, antiretroviral therapy (ART), public health approaches, and clinical guidelines. 1. Recommendations for a public health approach to the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating pregnant women and preventing HIV infection in infants were outlined in a WHO document accessed on May 15, 2013. 2. The 2006 revision of the WHO guidelines on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection in infants and children emphasized universal access and public health strategies. This document was accessed on May 15, 2013. 3. Gilks et al. discussed the WHO public health approach to antiretroviral therapy (ART) in resource-limited settings in a 2006 article published in The Lancet (Volume 368, Pages 505–510). 4. WHO guidelines on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection in adults and adolescents, focusing on public health recommendations, were accessed on May 15, 2013. 5. The 2010 revision of WHO recommendations for antiretroviral drugs in pregnant women and infants aimed at universal access was published in Geneva and accessed on May 15, 2013. 6. The strategic use of antiretrovirals for treatment and prevention of HIV infection was detailed in a WHO document accessed on May 15, 2013. 7. The United Nations General Assembly's 2006 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS, published in New York, outlined global commitments to addressing the epidemic. 8. The 2011 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS by the United Nations General Assembly focused on intensifying efforts to eliminate HIV and AIDS. 9. Guyatt et al. introduced the GRADE evidence profiles and summary of findings tables in a 2011 article in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Pages 383–394). 10. Guyatt et al. also discussed framing clinical questions and determining the importance of outcomes in the second GRADE guidelines article, published in the same journal (Volume 64, Pages 395–400). 11. Balshem et al. provided an introduction to rating the quality of evidence in the third GRADE guidelines article, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Pages 401–406). 12. Guyatt et al. addressed study limitations and risk of bias in the fourth GRADE guidelines article, published in the same journal (Volume 64, Pages 407–415). 13. The fifth GRADE guidelines article by Guyatt et al. focused on rating the quality of evidence for publication bias, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Pages 1277–1282). 14. The sixth GRADE guidelines article by Guyatt et al. discussed rating the quality of evidence for imprecision (random error), published in the same journal (Volume 64, Pages 1283–1293). 15. Guyatt et al. explored inconsistency in evidence quality in the seventh GRADE guidelines article, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Pages 1294–1302). 16. The eighth GRADE guidelines article by Guyatt et al. examined indirectness in evidence quality, published in the same journal (Volume 64, Pages 1303–1310). 17. The ninth GRADE guidelines article by Guyatt et al. focused on upgrading the quality of evidence, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Pages 1311–1316). 18. Andrews et al. discussed the process of translating evidence into recommendations in the fifteenth GRADE guidelines article, which was in press at the time. 19. Sweat et al. conducted a randomized study on community-based interventions to increase HIV testing and case detection in Tanzania, Zimbabwe, and Thailand, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases (2011, Volume 11, Pages 525–532). 20. Corbett et al. evaluated the uptake of workplace HIV counseling and testing in a cluster-randomized trial in Zimbabwe, published in PLoS Medicine (2006, Volume 3, Article e238). 21. Grabbe et al. analyzed strategies, utilization, and cost-effectiveness of mobile HIV counseling and testing services in Kenya, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (2010, Volume 54, Pages 317–323). 22. Granich et al. modeled the potential prevention impact of an integrated multi-disease prevention campaign for HIV and tuberculosis in Kenya, published in AIDS Research and Treatment (2012, Article 412643). 23. Lugada et al. compared home-based and clinic-based HIV testing among household members of individuals on ART in Uganda, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (2010, Volume 55, Pages 245–252). 24. Menzies et al. assessed the costs and effectiveness of four HIV counseling and testing strategies in Uganda, published in AIDS (2009, Volume 23, Pages 395–401). 25. van Schaik et al. explored the role of mobile services in earlier HIV diagnosis in South Africa, published in the South African Medical Journal (2010, Volume 100, Pages 671–674). 26. Wolff et al. evaluated a home-based voluntary counseling and testing intervention in rural Uganda, published in Health Policy and Planning (2005, Volume 20, Pages 109–116). 27. Bingham et al. reported HIV risk factors among male bathhouse attendees in Los Angeles, published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases (2008, Volume 35, Pages 631–636). 28. Lahuerta et al. compared users of community-based mobile HIV/syphilis screening vans with traditional voluntary counseling and testing sites in Guatemala, published in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2011, Volume 87, Pages 136–140). 29. Nhurod et al. examined access to HIV testing for sex workers in Bangkok, Thailand, highlighting a high prevalence of HIV among street-based sex workers, published in the Southeast Asian Journal of Tropical Medicine and Public Health (2010, Volume 41, Pages 153–162). 30. Kränzer et al. identified factors associated with HIV test refusal in rural Malawi, published in Tropical Medicine and International Health (2008, Volume 13, Pages 1341–1350). 31. Negin et al. evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and cost of home-based HIV testing in rural Kenya, published in Tropical Medicine and International Health (2009, Volume 14, Pages 849–855). 32. Chirawu et al. discussed the acceptability and challenges of implementing voluntary counseling and testing in rural Zimbabwe, published in AIDS Care (2010, Volume 22, Pages 81–88). 33. Ostermann et al. analyzed the uptake of mobile HIV counseling and testing in Tanzania's Kilimanjaro region, published in PLoS One (2011, Volume 6, Article e16488). 34. Choko et al. assessed the uptake and accuracy of oral kits for HIV self-testing in high-prevalence settings in Malawi, published in PLoS Medicine (2011, Volume 8, Article e1001102). 35. Frank et al. evaluated anonymous HIV testing using home collection and telemedicine counseling in a multicenter study, published in the Archives of Internal Medicine (1997, Volume 157, Pages 309–314). 36. Spielberg et al. examined the acceptability of home collection for frequent HIV testing using oral fluids and dried blood spots, published in AIDS (2000, Volume 14, Pages 1819–1828). 37. Feeley et al. described a successful workplace program for voluntary counseling, testing, and treatment of HIV/AIDS at Heineken in Rwanda, published in the International Journal of Occupational and Environmental Health (2007, Volume 13, Pages 99–106). 38. Outlaw et al. used motivational interviewing in HIV field outreach with young African American men who have sex with men, published in the American Journal of Public Health (2010, Volume 100, Supplement 1, Pages S146–S151). 39. Bell et al. discussed case finding for HIV-positive youth as a hidden population, published in the Journal of Adolescent Health (2003, Volume 33, Pages 10–22). 40. Champenois et al. described a community-based HIV testing intervention for men who have sex with men in nonmedical settings, published in BMJ Open (2012, Volume 2, Article e000693). 41. Morin et al. evaluated same-day mobile HIV testing in Zimbabwe, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (2006, Volume 41, Pages 218–224). 42. WHO provided guidance on HIV testing and counseling for adolescents and care for adolescents living with HIV in a 2013 document. 43. WHO also issued recommendations for the prevention and treatment of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections among sex workers in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing public health approaches. 44. Baeten et al. studied antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV prevention in heterosexual men and women, published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2012, Volume 367, Pages 399–410). 45. Grant et al. investigated pre-exposure chemoprophylaxis for HIV prevention in men who have sex with men, published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2010, Volume 363, Pages 2587–2599). 46. Thigpen et al. examined antiretroviral pre-exposure prophylaxis for heterosexual HIV transmission in Botswana, published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2012, Volume 367, Pages 423–434). 47. Choopanya et al. conducted a randomized trial on antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV in injecting drug users in Bangkok, published in The Lancet (2013, Volume 381, Pages 2083–2090). 48. WHO developed clinical and policy guidelines for responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women, which were in press at the time. 49. Weller and Davis-Beaty reviewed condom effectiveness in reducing heterosexual HIV transmission, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (2009, Issue 1, Article CD003255). 50. French et al. compared the use-effectiveness of female versus male condoms in preventing sexually transmitted diseases in women, published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases (2003, Volume 30, Pages 433–439). 51. Siegfried et al. reviewed male circumcision for the prevention of heterosexual acquisition of HIV in men, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (2009, Issue 2, Article CD003362). 52. Kränzer et al. systematically reviewed losses along the continuum of care for people living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society (2012, Volume 15, Pages 173–183). 53. Faal et al. demonstrated that providing immediate CD4 count results at HIV testing improves ART initiation, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (2011, Volume 58, Pages e54–e59). 54. Jani et al. evaluated the effect of point-of-care CD4 cell count tests on patient retention and ART initiation rates in primary health clinics, published in The Lancet (2011, Volume 378, Pages 1572–1579). 55. Gupta et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on early mortality in adults initiating ART in lowand middle-income countries, published in PLoS One (2011, Volume 6, Article e28691). 56. Brinkhof et al. compared mortality rates of HIV-infected patients starting ART in sub-Saharan Africa with HIV-unrelated mortality, published in PLoS Medicine (2009, Volume 6, Article e1000066). 57. Mocroft et al. studied the normalization of CD4 counts in HIV-1-infected patients with maximum virological suppression on combination ART, published in The Lancet (2007, Volume 370, Pages 407–413). 58. Haddow et al. investigated the incidence, clinical spectrum, risk factors, and impact of HIV-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in South Africa, published in PLoS One (2012, Volume 7, Article e40623). 59. Huis in ‘t Veld et al. reviewed the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome related to HIV co-infections, published in the European Journal of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (2012, Volume 31, Pages 919–927). 60. Vitoria et al. discussed scaling up ART in resource-limited settings and adapting guidance to meet challenges, published in Current Opinion in HIV and AIDS (2013, Volume 8, Pages 12–18). 61. Emery et al. analyzed major clinical outcomes in ART-naive participants and those not receiving ART at baseline in the SMART study, published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases (2008, Volume 197, Pages 1133–1144). 62. Severe et al. compared early versus standard ART initiation for HIV-infected adults in Haiti, published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2010, Volume 363, Pages 257–265). 63. Badri et al. assessed the revised WHO guidelines for scaling up ART in sub-Saharan Africa, published in AIDS (2004, Volume 18, Pages 1159–1168). 64. Moh et al. studied the incidence and determinants of mortality and morbidity following early ART initiation in West Africa, published in AIDS (2007, Volume 21, Pages 2483–2491). 65. Wong et al. established CD4 thresholds for ART initiation in a cohort of HIV-infected adults in Hong Kong, published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs (2007, Volume 21, Pages 106–115). 66. Sterne et al. analyzed the timing of ART initiation in AIDS-free HIV-1-infected patients across 18 cohort studies, published in The Lancet (2009, Volume 373, Pages 1352–1363). 67. Granich et al. proposed universal voluntary HIV testing with immediate ART as a strategy for eliminating HIV transmission, published in The Lancet (2009, Volume 373, Pages 48–57). 68. The 2011 Global HIV/AIDS response progress report provided an epidemic update and health sector progress toward universal access. 69. Mugglin et al. reviewed immunodeficiency at the start of ART globally, with findings accessible online as of May 15, 2013. 70. Egger et al. examined immunodeficiency at the start of combination ART in low-, middle-, and high-income countries, with findings in press. 71. Lessells et al. reported a reduction in early mortality on ART for adults in rural South Africa following changes in CD4+ cell count eligibility criteria, with findings in press. 72. Kowalska et al. developed a standardized algorithm for determining the underlying cause of death in HIV infection as AIDSor non-AIDS-related, published in HIV Clinical Trials (2011, Volume 12, Pages 109–117). 73. Moore et al. analyzed the rate of non-HIV/AIDS-related comorbidities among HIV-infected patients by CD4 cell count and HAART use status, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases (2008, Volume 47, Pages 1102–1104). 74. Baker et al. studied the relationship between CD4 count and the risk of non-AIDS diseases following initial HIV treatment, published in AIDS (2008, Volume 22, Pages 841–848). 75. Cohen et al. investigated the prevention of HIV-1 infection with early ART, with findings in press.
